samples.text:
The table shows the most popular countries where students from one country went to study abroad in 2012 and 2024, and it show the number of students and the share.

Overall, the total number of students increased from 56,000 to 72,800, and the United States was the most popular destination in both years, but its share became smaller.

In 2012, 21,400 students went to the United States, it was 38% of all students. This number decreased to 18,900 in 2024 and the share fell to 26%. The United Kingdom was the second in both years. The number of students increased from 12,300 to 15,300, however the share was almost same, 22% and 21%.

Canada had the biggest change. In 2012 only 5,600 students studied there, but in 2024 the number was 14,600 and the share went up from 10% to 20%. Australia also increased from 8,400 to 13,100 students. Germany was the least popular but the number of students more than doubled, from 2,800 to 5,800. Other countries was 5,500 in 2012 and 5,100 in 2024.
samples.why: Relevant overview and accurate figures · key changes identified but presented as a list with limited comparison · repetitive vocabulary · comma splices and agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The table compares the numbers and proportions of students from one country who went abroad to study in the five most popular destinations in 2012 and 2024.

Overall, the total number of international students grew considerably over the period. Although the United States remained the leading destination, its dominance declined, while Canada experienced the most significant growth.

The total rose from 56,000 in 2012 to 72,800 in 2024. In the first year, the US attracted 21,400 students, accounting for 38% of the total, but by 2024 this figure had fallen to 18,900, or just 26%. The United Kingdom was the second most popular choice in both years, with student numbers rising from 12,300 to 15,300, although its share stayed almost unchanged at around a fifth.

Canada saw a remarkable increase, with the number of students choosing it rising from 5,600 to 14,600. As a result, its share doubled from 10% to 20%, and it overtook Australia, which also grew from 8,400 to 13,100 students. Germany was the least popular of the named destinations, but its numbers more than doubled to 5,800, raising its share from 5% to 8%. Meanwhile, the number going to other countries fell slightly, from 5,500 to 5,100.
samples.why: Clear overview of overall growth and shifting shares · numbers and percentages linked effectively · logical progression · good lexical range (dominance, overtook) · frequent error-free sentences, slight repetition of rising.

samples.text:
The table presents data on the five leading study-abroad destinations for students from one country, giving both the number of students and each destination's share of the total in 2012 and 2024.

The most notable development is that, while overall numbers rose substantially, the United States lost much of its dominance, with Canada emerging as the fastest-growing destination. As a result, students in 2024 were spread far more evenly across the main countries.

Between the two years, the total number of students studying overseas increased by 16,800, from 56,000 to 72,800. The United States was the only major destination to attract fewer students, as its intake slipped from 21,400 to 18,900, causing its share to shrink from 38% to 26%. The United Kingdom, in second place in both years, gained 3,000 students, reaching 15,300, yet its share remained virtually stable at 21–22%.

Canada's rise was particularly striking: its student numbers grew more than two and a half times, from 5,600 to 14,600, doubling its share to 20% and lifting it above Australia (13,100). Germany, though still the smallest named destination, also more than doubled its intake to 5,800, whereas the figure for other countries edged down from 5,500 to 5,100.
samples.why: Perceptive overview on the more even spread of students · absolute and proportional data integrated skilfully · cohesion effortless · precise vocabulary (slipped, edged down) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
